highlights: Launched on 20 August 1975 on a Titan IIIE-Centaur rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Reached orbit around Mars on 19 June 1976. Its landing, first planned for 4 July, was delayed to find a safer spot.
Minutes after touchdown it took the first-ever photo from the surface of Mars: a close-up of its own footpad.
Its orbiter partner kept circling Mars and mapping the planet until 7 August 1980.
Its record of more than six years working on Mars lasted until the Opportunity rover beat it in 2010.

links.title: HiRISE: Viking Lander 1 seen from orbit

highlights: Launched on 9 September 1975 on a Titan IIIE-Centaur rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Reached orbit around Mars on 7 August 1976, then spent weeks scouting for a safe landing spot.
It landed thousands of kilometers from its twin, Viking 1, much farther north.
Its seismometer was the first to work on Mars, though wind shaking the lander made marsquakes hard to spot.
Its orbiter partner was switched off on 25 July 1978 after a fuel leak.
The lander was later renamed the Gerald Soffen Memorial Station, after the Viking project scientist.

links.title: HiRISE: Viking Lander 2 seen from orbit

highlights: Launched on 4 December 1996 on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
After a seven-month trip it flew straight into the Martian air without stopping in orbit first.
Wrapped in airbags, it bounced about 15 times across the ground before rolling to a stop.
Together with Sojourner it sent home about 2.3 billion bits of data, including millions of weather readings.
NASA declared the mission over on 4 November 1997, after weeks of trying to reach the silent lander.
HiRISE photographed the lander from orbit in December 2006, almost ten years after it landed.
Launched on 4 December 1996, folded up on the Pathfinder lander, on a Delta II rocket.
It rolled down a ramp onto Mars on 5 July 1997 (US time), the day after landing.
It weighed only about 10.6 kg and crept along at about 1 centimeter per second.
It drove about 100 meters in total, zig-zagging between rocks near the lander.
It sent back about 550 pictures and studied the chemistry of rocks and soil.
It worked for 83 Mars days, about 12 times longer than its planned 7 days.
Launched on 10 June 2003 on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Less than three weeks after landing a memory problem froze it; engineers fixed it by radio from Earth.
In August 2005 it climbed to the top of Husband Hill, with a view across Gusev crater.
Its right front wheel stopped turning in March 2006, so it drove backwards, dragging the broken wheel.
Martian whirlwinds called dust devils sometimes blew dust off its solar panels, giving it surprise power boosts.
It drove about 7.7 km in total before getting stuck at Troy.

highlights: Launched on 7 July 2003 (Florida time) on a Delta II Heavy rocket from Cape Canaveral.
It rolled to a stop inside a small crater called Eagle, a lucky landing nicknamed a 'hole in one'.
In January 2005 it found 'Heat Shield Rock', the first meteorite ever identified on another planet.
From 2006 to 2008 it explored Victoria crater, driving down inside it and back out.
On 9 August 2011 it reached the rim of giant Endeavour crater after a three-year drive.
In July 2014 it beat the Soviet Lunokhod 2 rover's record for the longest drive on another world.

highlights: Launched on 4 August 2007 on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
It was built partly from a lander that was shelved after Mars Polar Lander was lost in 1999.
HiRISE photographed it hanging from its parachute, the first picture of a spacecraft landing on another world.
On 31 July 2008 its tiny ovens heated a soil sample and confirmed it contained water ice.
Planned for 90 Mars days, it worked for about five months before winter darkness arrived.

highlights: Launched on 5 May 2018 on an Atlas V from Vandenberg, California: the first US planetary launch from the West Coast.
Two briefcase-sized satellites called MarCO flew alongside and radioed news of its landing back to Earth.
Its robotic arm set the seismometer down on the ground on 19 December 2018.
It detected its first marsquake on 6 April 2019.
Its heat probe, nicknamed 'the mole', could not dig deep, and the team stopped trying in January 2021.
On 24 December 2021 it felt a meteoroid hit; orbiters then found the new crater, with chunks of ice.
Launched on 30 July 2020, tucked under Perseverance, on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral.
Perseverance dropped it gently onto the ground on 3 April 2021.
It weighs only about 1.8 kg, and its blades spin about 2,400 times a minute to grip the thin air.
On 26 February 2022 HiRISE spotted it from orbit, about 200 meters from Perseverance.
Over 72 flights it flew about 17 km and spent a little over two hours in the air.

highlights: Launched on 3 January 1999 on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
It carried the first microphone ever sent to Mars, meant to record Martian sounds.
It arrived at Mars on 3 December 1999 after an 11-month trip.
A NASA review board reported on the most likely cause of the loss in March 2000.
Orbiter cameras have searched its target area many times, but its wreck has never been confirmed.

highlights: Launched on 3 January 1999, riding on Mars Polar Lander's cruise stage, on a Delta II rocket.
They were part of NASA's New Millennium Program, which tested new technology for future missions.
The probes were named Amundsen and Scott, after the first explorers to reach Earth's South Pole.
Each probe weighed about 3.6 kg, roughly as much as a house cat.
They were aimed at icy layered ground near 73 degrees south, close to Mars's south pole.
Building both probes cost about 29 million US dollars.

highlights: Launched on 11 December 1998 on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
It carried a color weather camera and an infrared sounder to measure the Martian air.
On 10 November 1999 a NASA board published its report naming the unit mix-up as the cause.
A copy of its weather instrument later flew to Mars on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, launched in 2005.

highlights: Launched on 26 November 2011 on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
In September 2012 it found rounded pebbles from an ancient stream that once flowed in Gale crater.
In September 2014 it reached the base of Mount Sharp, its main goal.
In June 2018 scientists announced it had found organic molecules in 3-billion-year-old rocks.
In May 2024 it drove over a rock, cracked it open and revealed yellow crystals of pure sulfur.
In March 2025 scientists reported the largest organic molecules yet found on Mars, in a Curiosity sample.

highlights: Launched on 30 July 2020 on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
While landing it used Terrain-Relative Navigation, matching camera views to a map to steer away from hazards.
Its landing spot was named Octavia E. Butler Landing, after the science-fiction author.
On 20 April 2021 its MOXIE experiment made oxygen from Martian air, a first on another planet.
On 6 September 2021 it sealed its first rock core sample in a tube.
In December 2022 and January 2023 it left ten sample tubes at a backup depot called Three Forks.

highlights: The parachute opened at supersonic speed, about 11 km above the ground.
HiRISE photographed Perseverance drifting under this parachute during the landing on 18 February 2021.
The backshell is about 4.5 meters wide, wider than a car is long.
Space fans cracked the parachute's hidden code within hours after NASA showed it on 22 February 2021.
